name: Karl Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thank you for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we're not selling anything. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Is that all right?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: That's fine. I've done one of these surveys before, though that one was about the milk price.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Good. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm up at half four, in the parlour by five with Dev, my herdsman, and we milk 250 cows before breakfast. Then it's the team meeting at the kitchen table at seven, six of us, and I hand out the day: who's on the barley, who's fixing the slurry pump, who's taking the calves. I love the cows and I love a good harvest; what wears me out is the co-op's paperwork and the endless forms.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Who owns the farm, and what's your part in it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The dairy co-op owns Hollow Lane, about 300 hectares with the grass, and I'm the farm manager. I've a degree in agriculture and I've been here fourteen years. I live in the village with Mira, who's a district nurse, and our two, Anya and Theo, with a mortgage we'll be paying for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. Now I'll read you five short pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I've said for years: the clever stuff never reaches the cowshed. The co-op sent us a feed app two winters ago and I still write the rations in my notebook. At the union branch meeting I'd tell people to stop worrying about machines and start worrying about the milk price.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it means very little for me. I run Hollow Lane Farm for the dairy co-op, 250 cows and about 300 hectares of barley, wheat and grass, and none of that gets done by a computer. My pay is good, Mira's nursing job is steady, and we've got a fair bit put by.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on, and I mean that. I'd push the co-op board for the new pay scale for my team of six before the spring calving, because that's a fight worth having anyway. And I'd keep paying a bit extra off the mortgage each month like we already do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. The things that keep me awake are a wet harvest or a bad case of mastitis in the herd, not software. I'd feel a bit smug, if I'm honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the milk price. If nothing changes with AI, what does still worry you about the next few years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The milk price, the bank rate and the co-op getting bought by a bigger outfit. Two neighbouring farms went to a big dairy group last year and the first thing they did was cut the staff housing. That's a worry with or without any AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work do you think about when you picture this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev, my herdsman, who's been with me eleven years. Dev has three kids and lives in a co-op cottage. If anything goes wrong, my first job is making sure Dev keeps his house and his hours.

say: I'd say the **clever stuff** never reaches the cowshed, so people should calm down.
I'd tell the **union branch** to worry about the milk price, not machines.
think: I think it means **very little** for me, because nobody runs 250 cows from a screen.
My **pay**, Mira's nursing job and our **savings** already feel solid.
do: Push the co-op board for a **new pay scale** for my team before spring calving.
Keep paying a **bit extra** off the mortgage each month, as we do now.
feel: Mostly **calm**, with a touch of **smugness** about the hype.
S0.quote: The co-op sent us a feed app two winters ago and I still write the rations in my notebook.
fieldNote: He runs a **co-op-owned dairy** and arable farm and treats AI as office talk.
His real worries are **milk price**, interest rates and a takeover of the co-op.
His first instinct is to protect **Dev**, his herdsman, and the staff housing.

steps.text: Push the co-op board for a new pay scale before spring calving
Keep running the herd and the barley the same way

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the office staff at the co-op headquarters are the ones in trouble, not us out in the yard. I'd post something on the union page saying any software the co-op brings in should come with a deal for the staff it replaces. That's the bit people forget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it creeps closer than I'd like. The co-op already wants me to log every calving and every spray on a tablet, and in this picture the tablet starts telling me what to do. I'd still be needed for the cows, but I'd be a pair of hands taking orders from a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to the branch meeting in January and get a motion passed that nobody on the farm team is cut because of software without a year's notice. I'd keep doing the rations by hand and let the young assistant, Josie, do the tablet bits. We'd also keep putting about 600 a month into savings instead of buying the new pickup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job looks safe for now, but I can feel the ground moving under the co-op. I don't like being told how to farm by a programme somebody wrote in a city.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd let Josie do the tablet work. What happens if the co-op says the farm manager has to use it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd use it badly and complain loudly, which is not my proudest answer. I'm good with cows and soil, I'm hopeless with passwords. If it came down to it I'd ask Mira to sit with me on a Sunday and walk me through it, the way she does with her patient system.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Josie, oddly, even though she's the one who likes the tablet. If the planning and the ordering go to software, the co-op won't need an assistant manager to do them. Josie is twenty-four and wants my job one day, and there might not be a ladder left for her to climb.

say: I'd say the **co-op office** staff are in trouble before anyone out in the yard.
I'd post that any new software must come with a **deal for staff** it replaces.
think: I think the tablet will start **giving orders** and I'll become a pair of hands.
My **own job** is safe for now, but the co-op around me is changing.
do: Get a **union motion** passed in January demanding a year's notice before software-driven cuts.
Keep putting about **600 a month** into savings instead of buying a new pickup.
feel: **Uneasy** about losing control of how the farm is run.
S1.quote: I'm good with cows and soil, I'm hopeless with passwords.
fieldNote: He sees **desk jobs** at the co-op hit first and his own role safe, for now.
His resistance shows: he'd **hand the tablet** to his assistant rather than learn it.
He worries most about **Josie**, the young assistant, losing a ladder to climb.
He turns to the **union** as his first tool, even in a mild scenario.

steps.text: Pass a union motion asking for a year's notice before software cuts
Put about 600 a month into savings instead of buying a pickup
Keep writing feed rations by hand and leave the tablet to Josie

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need laws before it lands, not after. I'd stand up at the branch meeting and say the government has to make the companies that own these robots pay into a fund for the people they replace. I'd be angry and I'd say so in public.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I lose my job, maybe not in 2028 but by 2031 or soon after. The planning, the ordering and the herd records go to the machine first, and the co-op board will start asking why they pay a manager. Then the robots arrive for the milking and the tractor work and the whole team goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now, I'd stop the extra mortgage payments and build cash instead, because cash is what you need when you're out of work. I'd get the union to push for a retraining fund paid by the robot makers, and I'd write to our member of parliament every month. And I'd sit Anya down, she's twelve, and tell her to look at nursing like her mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Sick in the stomach, honestly. I've done this since I was a boy and I'm among the best at it, and none of that would matter. I can't picture what I'd do on a Monday morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The thinking AI comes in 2028 and the robots about three years later. What do those three years mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those three years are the worst bit, because I'd know what's coming and still be milking every morning. In the first year the machine does my planning and Josie's job disappears. Then I'd be the man out in the yard watching the co-op order robots and knowing I'm next.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've got savings and Mira earns a steady wage. Does that change how bad this feels?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we don't lose the house, and I'm grateful for that. Mira's work is caring for people, and I can't see a robot giving an old man his insulin any time soon. My kids would be fine, but I'd be a 48-year-old man with no trade, and money doesn't fix that.

say: I'd say we need **laws before it lands**, not after the damage is done.
I'd demand that **robot owners pay** into a fund for the workers they replace.
think: I think I **lose my job** by 2031, once the board stops needing a manager.
The **planning and ordering** go first, then the robots take the milking and fieldwork.
do: Stop the **extra mortgage payments** and build up cash for when the work stops.
Push the union for a **retraining fund** and write to our MP every month.
Tell **Anya** to look seriously at nursing, like her mother.
feel: **Sick** at the thought of losing the work he's best at.
**Grateful** that Mira's job keeps the house safe.
S2.quote: I'd be the man out in the yard watching the co-op order robots and knowing I'm next.
fieldNote: He expects to **lose his job** by about 2031 and has no plan for afterwards.
He blames the **robot owners** and wants them to fund the people they replace.
The **three-year gap** feels like slow torture to him, not breathing room.
**Mira's job** and their savings protect the house, but not his sense of purpose.

steps.text: Stop extra mortgage payments and build cash in the bank
Push the union for a retraining fund paid by robot makers
Write to the local MP every month about a replacement fund
Talk to Anya about training as a nurse like her mother

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thanks. The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Like with the fast one, I'd say get the rules written now while there's time. Five years is enough for a government to do something if it wants to. I'd say that at the branch and at the pub.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, it's the same ending, just with a bit more runway. The board would start trimming in about 2031 and the robots would be milking by about 2034, when I'm 51. That gives me time to save, but I still can't see myself doing anything other than farming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first two or three years I'd mostly carry on and watch, honestly, because I don't trust predictions. I'd keep building savings, maybe 800 a month. And I'd get the union to set up a farm staff group that talks to the co-op board every quarter about how the machines come in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with a bit of air. Five years feels like enough to get some protection in place. It still ends with me out of a job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd mostly carry on and watch. Is that a plan or a way of not thinking about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bit of both, if I'm honest with you. Mira says I always wait until the cow is calving before I go and get the ropes. I'd want to see the first robot milking somebody else's herd before I believed it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Dev, your herdsman, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Dev straight that the co-op will want the cottages back once the herd is run by machines. I'd tell Dev to save hard and get his name on a housing list now. That's a hard conversation over a sandwich in the tractor.

say: I'd say **write the rules now**, while there are five years to do it.
I'd say it at the **union branch** and at the pub, to anyone who'd listen.
think: I think it's the **same ending** with a bit more runway before it hits me.
I'd be **51** when the robots arrive, and I can't see another trade.
do: Save about **800 a month** while watching what happens on other farms.
Set up a **farm staff group** that meets the co-op board every quarter.
feel: **Anxious**, but with some air to breathe.
Still sure it ends with **no job**.
S3.quote: Mira says I always wait until the cow is calving before I go and get the ropes.
fieldNote: He admits his **waiting** is partly avoidance, which his partner points out often.
He needs to **see a robot** milking someone else's herd before he'll believe it.
His concern for **Dev's cottage** shows how housing ties farm workers to the job.

steps.text: Save about 800 a month while watching neighbouring farms
Set up a staff group that meets the co-op board quarterly
Wait to see a robot milking another herd before changing anything

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Thank you. The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift and we'd be fools to waste it. I'd tell people at the branch that this is the time to win a shorter working week and a proper share of what the machines earn. Public money should go into retraining farm workers, not into subsidising robot leases.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd still be 56 when the robots arrive in 2039, and that's not retirement age. I'd probably keep the job longer than most, because the co-op will want one person who knows the land. But I'd be managing machines, not people, and I'm not sure I want that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep farming and keep saving, and I'd pay the mortgage off by about 2034 so it's gone before anything hits. I'd get properly involved in the party locally, door-knocking for candidates who back a robot tax. And we'd steer Theo, who's nine, toward something with people, maybe teaching or a trade like electrician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy more than scared, but anxious underneath. Ten years sounds long until you count it in calving seasons, and a dairy farmer only gets ten more springs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten springs. What does that change about how you farm right now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want to make those ten springs count, honestly. I'd teach Josie everything I know about reading a field by looking at it, because that knowledge dies with me otherwise. And I'd stop putting off the hedge-planting I've been meaning to do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You don't use AI tools at all now. Would ten years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably not much, I'll be honest. I'd learn the minimum to keep my job, the way I learned the milking parlour computer in 2015, grumbling. I'm not going to become a tech person at 50.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift** and wasting it would be foolish.
I'd push for a **shorter working week** and a fair share of machine earnings.
think: I'd still be **56** in 2039, which is well short of retirement age.
I'd likely become a **manager of machines** rather than people, which I don't want.
do: Pay off the **mortgage** by about 2034, before the robots arrive.
Door-knock for local candidates who back a **robot tax**.
Steer **Theo** toward teaching or an electrician's trade.
feel: **Uneasy** on the surface and **anxious** underneath about the countdown.
S4.quote: Ten years sounds long until you count it in calving seasons, and a dairy farmer only gets ten more springs.
fieldNote: He counts time in **calving seasons**, which makes ten years feel short.
He would learn only the **bare minimum** of new tech to keep his job.
He wants to pass on his **field knowledge** to Josie before it is lost.

steps.text: Pay off the house mortgage by about 2034
Door-knock for local candidates who back a robot tax
Steer Theo toward teaching or an electrician's apprenticeship
Keep running the herd and teach Josie to read the fields

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, without a doubt, because it would take my job before I'd even worked out what to do instead. What would help is a fund paid by the robot makers that pays farm workers to retrain on full wages, and a law that protects tied cottages like Dev's. I don't want charity; I want a share of what these machines make from our land.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who decides. Every picture assumes the machines just arrive, but somebody on a board somewhere chooses to buy them. If farm workers had a seat on that board, the whole thing would look different.

headlineQuote: Every picture assumes the machines just arrive, but somebody on a board somewhere chooses to buy them.
portrait: Karl, 43, manages a **co-op-owned dairy** and arable farm with a team of six.
He is among the **best farmers** around but avoids new tech and writes rations by hand.
He blames **boards and robot owners**, not the machines, and reaches for the union first.
He moves from **calm** in AI Plateau to **alarmed** in AGI by 2028.
His partner's **nursing job** and their savings protect the house but not his purpose.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries him most, because he'd lose his job before planning anything.
whatWouldHelp: A **retraining fund** paid by robot makers, with full wages during training.
A law protecting **tied cottages** and a worker seat on the board deciding on machines.
